title: Krylov Methods are (nearly) Optimal for Low-Rank Approximation
authors: Ainesh Bakshi (Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA), Shyam Narayanan (Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA)
abstract: We consider the problem of rank-$1$ low-rank approximation (LRA) in the matrix-vector product model under various Schatten norms: $\min_{ \|u\|_2=1} \left\|A (I - u u^\top)\right\|_{\mathcal{S}_p}$, where $\|M\|_{\mathcal{S}_p}$ denotes the $\ell_p$ norm of the singular values of $M$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, our goal is to output a unit vector $v$ such that $\left\|A (I - v v^\top)\right\|_{\mathcal{S}_p} \leq (1+\varepsilon) \min_{ \|u\|_2=1} \left\|A (I - u u^\top)\right\|_{\mathcal{S}_p}$. Our main result shows that Krylov methods (nearly) achieve the information-theoretically optimal number of matrix-vector products for Spectral ($p=\infty$), Frobenius ($p=2$) and Nuclear ($p=1$) LRA. In particular, for Spectral LRA, we show that any algorithm requires $\Omega(\log(n)/\varepsilon^{1/2})$ matrix-vector products, exactly matching the upper bound obtained by Krylov methods (Musco and Musco, 2015). Our lower bound addresses Open Question 1 in (Woodruff, 2014), providing evidence for the lack of progress on algorithms for Spectral LRA and resolves Open Question 1.2 in (Bakshi et al., 2022). Next, we show that for any fixed constant $p$, i.e. $1\leq p =O(1)$, there is an upper bound of $O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^{1/3})$ matrix-vector products, implying that the complexity does not grow as a function of input size. This improves the $O(\log(n/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^{1/3})$ bound recently obtained in (Bakshi et al., 2022), and matches their $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^{1/3})$ lower bound, to a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Iterative algorithms are the workhorse of modern optimization methods and are pervasive throughout scientiﬁc computing, numerical linear algebra and machine learning. Such
algorithms are now used for a wide array of tasks, from
training large machine learning models [9], [23], running
large-scale simulations for ﬂuid dynamics [18]–[20], structural
analysis [49], [57] and computational chemistry [52], [61],
to quantum machine learning [22], [25]. In order to develop
a general theory of iterative algorithms, and systematically

that simulatenously captures all such algorithms and admits
ﬁne-grained lower bounds. While the standard RAM model
easily captures iterative algorithms, we have no tools to obtain
ﬁne-grained lower bounds on their performace.
An alternate computational model that has recieved significant attention lately is the matrix-vector product model [5],
[10], [39], [43], [47], [54], [55], [58]. Here, the algorithm
accesses an input matrix A only via adaptive matrix-vector
queries. In particular, the algorithm chooses a query vector
v1 , obtains the product A · v1 , chooses the next query vector
v2 , which is any randomized function of v1 and A·v1 , receives
A · v2 , and so on. The fundametal measure of complexity in
this model is the minimum number of matrix-vector products
required to solve a given problem, which we refer to as the
matrix-vector complexity.
The matrix-vector product model captures natural iterative
algorithms and has been extensively studied in the scientiﬁc
computing and numerical linear algebra communities (see,
for instance, [29], and references therein). Further, in many
real-world applications, the number of matrix-vector products
dominate the overall running time [36]. Finally, it is possible
to obtain unconditional, information-theoretical lower bounds
on the matrix-vector complexity for various problems, as
demonstrated by [10], [54], for computing the top eigenvalue
of a matrix.
A popular class of iterative algorithms are based on computing the Krylov subspace: we loosely refer to such algorithms
as Krylov subspace methods. Here, instead of discarding
intermediate matrix-vector products, the algorithm constructs
a basis for the subspace spanned by intermediate vectors,
i.e. K = [v, Av, A2 v, . . . At v]. Canonical examples of Krylov
subspace methods include Krylov iteration (Algorithm 13) to
compute top-k eigenvalues and low-rank approximations [24],
[40], [48], Conjugate Gradient to solve a linear system, and
Lanczos iteration to apply low-degree polynomials to eigenvalues (see [51] and references therein).
In this work, we focus on understanding the matrix-vector
complexity of low-rank approximation, in the special case
where the target rank is 1. In particular, given an n × d matrix
A and accuracy parameter 0 < ε < 1, the goal is to compute

Finally, we highlight a lifting theorem that shows under
fairly general conditions, a lower bound against Krylov iteration with large block size translates to an informationtheoretic lower bound against adaptive queries in the matrixvector model, which may be of independent interest. This
lifting result comes from concurrent work by Chewi, Dios
Pont, Li, Lu, and Narayanan [13]2 . We provide a simpliﬁed
description of the lifting result here.
Theorem 8 (Lifting Block Krylov Lower Bounds). Let A be
any adaptive algorithm that makes k matrix-vector queries to
an n × n symmetric matrix A, where the eigenvectors of A are
uniformly (Haar-)random. Then, given k random Gaussians
V = [v1 , . . . , vk ], one can perfectly simulate the distribution of
k adaptive queries and responses for A, given just the Krylov
matrix K = [AV, A2 V, A3 V, . . . Ak V ] and no other knowledge
of A.
At a high-level, this result shows that if there exists any
matrix-vector algorithm can solve a given eigenvalue or eigenvector problem with k adaptive queries, then Krylov iteration
with block size k can be used to solve the same problem
with k iterations. In general, this simulator requires k 2 matrixvector products, as opposed to k matrix-vector products used
by the adaptive algorithm, resulting in a quadratic overhead.
However, in the setting of Spectral LRA, we demonstrate that
starting with block size larger than 1 adds no value, and the
lifting technique obtains an optimal lower bound.
Remark 9. We note [13] proved a slightly simpler version
of Theorem 8, as they only require the lifting for solving
a problem that depends on the eigenvalues (speciﬁcally, estimating Tr(A−1 ), for the purpose of generating a sample
from N (0, A−1 )). However, our lower bound for low-rank
approximation is based on identifying good eigenvectors, so
Theorem 8 is in fact a slight generalization of their result.

II. T ECHNICAL OVERVIEW
In this section, we begin by describing our hard instance
and provide a complete proof of a lower bound against Krylov
Iteration (Algorithm 13) for Spectral LRA. We then outline the
approach to establish a lower bound against Block Krylov and
explain how to lift a lower bound against Block Krylov to a
general matrix-vector product lower bound. Finally, we discuss
the new ideas we require to obtain a better upper bound for
Schatten-p LRA, when p is a ﬁxed constant.

B. Lifting Krylov Lower Bounds to Matrix-Vector Lower
Bounds
In Section √II-A, we described why a Krylov subspace
with c log n/ ε iterations cannot approximately locate the
top eigenvector well enough to perform spectral LRA, for a
sufﬁciently small constant c. Perhaps surpsingly, it turns out,
that starting with a matrix instead of a single vector in Krylov
iteration does not√ help. In particular, we show that even if
we have c log
√ n/ ε starting vectors and run Krylov Iteration
for c log n/ ε iterations on each starting vector, the resulting
Krylov subspace does not contain any vector that is even εcorrelated with the top eigenvector of the input matrix.
In the single starting vector Krylov iteration lower bound,
we showed that for any unit vector w in the Krylov subspace,
|u1 , w | is very small. Intuitively, this should imply that for
block size S, a unit vector in the block Krylov subspace should
not have norm more than S · |u1 , w |. Indeed, we can write
w = w1 +w2 +· · ·+wS , where each wi comes from the Krylov
subspace generated by the i-th starting vector, so |u1 , w | ⩽
S
i=1 |u1 , wi  |.
The obstacle in excuting such an approach, however, is that
the vectors wi may be anti-correlated and cancel out. As a
result, it might be possible for some wi to have norm much
bigger than 1. We are able to overcome this obstacle and
show in our construction, with high probability, there is very
little anti-correlation between any potential wi and wj that
are chosen. This insight allows for our single-vector Krylov
iteration lower bound to extend to Block Krylov iteration.
Finally, we can apply the lifting
√ result to show that any
adaptive algorithm making log n/ ε queries can be simulated
by a Block Krylov algorithm. Intuitively, for an input instance
where the eigenvectors are a uniformly Haar random matrix,
the best an adaptive algorithm can do is to explore a uniformly
random direction in the complement of the subspace explored
thus far. We make this intuition precise by showing that the
sequence of adaptive queries can be modelled as {vi }i∈[k] ,




where vi = vi + vi⊥ , such that vi is the component of vi in
the span of the previous queries, and vi⊥ is orthogonal to this
span. Further, the distributon of vi⊥ is uniformly random over
the remaining subspace. We then show that Krylov iteration
with large block size can simulate such adaptive queries and
their responses.

III. A DDITIONAL R ELATED W ORK
In recent years, the matrix-vector product model has recieved considerable attention in the theoretical computer science community, since it was formalized for a number of
problems in [47], [55]. Simultaneously, [10], [54] obtained
nearly tight bounds for estimating the top eigenvector and
eigenvalue. Next, for the problem of estimating the trace of
a positive semideﬁnite matrix, tight bounds were obtained in
[39] (see, also [17] for estimating the diagonal). For recovering
a planted clique from a random graph, upper and lower
bounds were obtained in [46]. Finally, [5] studied the lowrank approximation problem and [43] studied testing whether
a matrix is PSD in the matrix-vector model.
A closely related setting to the matrix-vector model is
one where the input is accessed in a non-adaptive manner,
i.e. v1 , . . . , vq , are chosen before making any queries to A.
This model is equivalent to the sketching model, which is
thoroughly studied on its own (see, e.g., [45], [59]), and in
the context of data streams [31], [42]. Low-rank approximation
under Schatten norms has been well-studied in this model [15],
[35].
Iterative methods, such as Krylov subspace based methods,
are captured by the matrix-vector product framework, whereas
linear sketching allows for the choice of a matrix S ∈ Rt×n ,
where t is the number of “queries”, and then observes the
product S · A and so on (see [59] and references therein). The
model has important applications to streaming and distributed
algorithms and several recent works have focused on estimating spectral norms and the top singular values [1], [3], [30],
[33], estimating Schatten and Ky-Fan norms [11], [32]–[34]
and low-rank approximation [8], [15], [16], [37], [44].
Finally, the matrix-vector product model is also closely related to sublinear time/query algorithms and quantum-inspired
algorithms. There has been a ﬂurry of work on sublinear lowrank approximation under various structural assumptions on
the input [4], [7], [26], [41], [53] and in quantum-inspired
models [6], [12], [14], [21], [22], [28], [56].

Here, we know that the number of singular values in the range
[1/2, 1 − ε] is at most O(ε−1/3 ). We therefore construct an
entirely different polynomial, which is no longer based on
Chebyshev polynomials. This polynomial is designed to explicitly zero out all singular values in the range [1/2, 1−ε]. We
note that the degree of this polynomial, p0 , is only O(ε−1/3 ),
and it allows us to remove the contribution of all medium sized
singular values, similar to starting with a larger block size. This
polynomial construction is reminiscent of the polynomial used
by Saad [50] to analyze block Lanczos. However, it may still
be the case that p0 (σ1 ) is signiﬁcantly smaller than p0 (σj ),
for some σj outside the interval [1/2, 1 − ε].
